title: In Joshua 3 How Can We Create Memorials In Our Own Lives To Remember Gods Faithfulness
paragraphs: Remembering God’s Faithfulness: Lessons from Joshua 3

The third chapter of Joshua presents a pivotal moment in Israel’s history. The Israelites, after wandering in the wilderness for forty years, are about to cross the Jordan River into the Promised Land. God performs a miracle by stopping the waters of the Jordan, allowing His people to cross on dry ground—a powerful demonstration of His faithfulness and power. But God’s instructions go beyond the miracle itself; He commands the people to create a memorial so future generations will not forget His mighty works.
The Biblical Event: Crossing the Jordan and Building a Memorial

After the priests carrying the Ark of the Covenant step into the Jordan, the waters are miraculously halted. Once the entire nation has crossed, God instructs Joshua to select twelve men, one from each tribe, to take stones from the riverbed and set them up as a memorial:

And it shall come to pass, when your children shall ask their fathers in time to come, saying, What mean ye by these stones? then ye shall let your children know, saying, Israel came over this Jordan on dry land. - Joshua 4:21 ASV
This act of remembrance was not just for those who had witnessed the event, but for future generations as well.
The Importance of Memorials in the Life of Faith
Throughout Scripture, God’s people are called to remember His deeds. Memorials serve several vital purposes:
They remind us of God’s faithfulness and power. When we recall specific instances where God has worked in our lives, our faith is strengthened for future challenges.
They provide opportunities to share with others. Memorials prompt questions and conversations, allowing us to testify to God’s grace and goodness (Psalm 78:4 ASV).
They help us obey the biblical command to remember. Forgetting God’s works can lead to spiritual drift and ingratitude (Deuteronomy 8:11-14 ASV).
Practical Ways to Create Memorials Today
While we may not build stone altars, there are meaningful ways to establish memorials in our lives:
Journaling: Write down answered prayers, significant moments of God’s provision, and spiritual milestones. When times are difficult, review these entries to remember God’s faithfulness.
Celebrating Anniversaries: Mark important dates when God intervened—such as a healing, conversion, or deliverance—with a time of prayer and thanksgiving.
Sharing Testimonies: Tell your story to your family, friends, or church. Verbal testimony can be a living memorial for both the speaker and the listener (Psalm 107:2 ASV).
Physical Reminders: Keep an item that represents a significant event—such as a stone, photo, or note—in a visible place to prompt gratitude and remembrance.
Family Traditions: Establish regular practices, such as reading specific Bible passages or singing certain hymns, to commemorate God’s goodness through the years.
The Centrality of Christ in Our Memorials
As believers, our greatest memorial is the cross and resurrection of Jesus Christ. Jesus instituted the Lord’s Supper as a memorial of His sacrifice:
This do in remembrance of me. - Luke 22:19 ASV
Every time we partake of communion, we are reminded of the ultimate act of God’s faithfulness—the redemption accomplished by Christ (1 Corinthians 11:26 ASV).
Conclusion: Building a Legacy of Remembrance

Just as the Israelites built a memorial to remember the crossing of the Jordan, we are called to intentionally remember and recount God’s faithfulness in our own lives. By doing so, we nurture our own faith and pass down a legacy of trust in God to those who come after us. Let us be diligent in creating “memorials” that point to the goodness and power of our faithful God.
